readerTitle: The biggest order that hurt: why gatekeepers set the terms
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (Vlasic 피클과 대형 소매점, 언론 보도 기반) + 가상 사례 (핫소스 제조사, 피트니스 앱)
insight: 게이트키퍼의 힘은 그들이 가진 고객 수가 아니라, 내가 가진 다른 문의 수가 얼마나 적은가에서 나온다.
misconception: 가장 큰 유통 채널에 들어가는 것이 곧 성공이다. 판매량이 늘면 이익도 따라 늘어난다.

sources.text: Fishman, C. (2003). The Wal-Mart You Don't Know. Fast Company, December 2003. (Vlasic gallon-jar pickle story)
U.S. Federal Trade Commission (2003). Slotting Allowances in the Retail Grocery Industry.
핫소스·피트니스 앱 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Vlasic 1갤런 피클 $2.97 판매 이야기는 Fast Company 2003년 기사(Charles Fishman)에 나옵니다. 원문의 가격과 맥락을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 기사에 대한 Walmart·Vlasic 측 반론이 있었는지도 확인이 필요합니다.
Vlasic Foods International은 2001년 파산 보호를 신청했습니다. 파산 원인은 여러 가지(분사 당시 부채, 다른 사업부 부진 등)이며, 피클 거래가 주원인이라고 단정하지 않도록 카드에 'one of many factors'로 적었습니다. 연도를 재확인하세요.
슬로팅 피(입점비)는 미국 식료품 유통에서 FTC가 조사한 관행입니다. 금액은 업체·품목마다 크게 달라 카드에 수치를 적지 않았습니다.
앱스토어 수수료율은 시기·프로그램·지역 규제에 따라 달라 카드에는 'a commission on many sales'로만 적었습니다. 특정 수수료율을 추가할 경우 공식 문서로 확인하세요.

cards.title: A gallon of pickles for $2.97
body: In the late 1990s, pickle maker Vlasic landed what looked like a dream deal: a giant gallon jar, sold by the biggest retailer in America for under three dollars.
It sold enormously well. According to a widely read 2003 report, it also helped squeeze the profit out of Vlasic's business.

image.label: A huge jar of pickles on a store shelf with a tiny price tag
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거대한 피클 유리병이 마트 선반을 가득 채우고, 아주 작은 가격표 "$2.97"가 붙어 있음. 병 옆에 작은 제조사 직원이 걱정스럽게 올려다봄. 실제 브랜드 로고나 매장 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A national chain wants your hot sauce.
body: You make hot sauce and sell it through 40 independent shops and your own website. A national grocery chain offers to stock it in 900 stores.
Their terms: a fee to get on the shelf, a lower wholesale price, regular promotions you pay for, and payment 60 days after delivery. What do you do?

options.text: Sign. 900 stores is the break you've been waiting for
options.feedback: You gain huge reach, but if the chain becomes most of your sales, every future term they set is one you can't refuse.

options.text: Start with one region and keep the chain under a set share of sales
options.feedback: You learn whether the deal actually makes money while keeping other doors open, which keeps your bargaining power. It grows slower.

options.text: Decline and stay with independent shops
options.feedback: You keep control and margin, but you may cap your growth and leave the shelf to a rival who says yes.

cards.title: The order was huge. The margin wasn't.
body: As reported, the gallon jar sold in large volumes, but Vlasic earned very little on each one. Shoppers who bought a whole gallon also stopped buying Vlasic's smaller, more profitable jars.
Pulling back was hard. The retailer was a big share of Vlasic's sales, and it could shift shelf space to other brands.
Vlasic filed for bankruptcy in 2001. The pickle deal was **one of many factors**, not the only cause. But it shows how a win at the door can still cost you inside.

cards.title: Gatekeepers
body: A **gatekeeper** is anyone who controls access to the customers you need: a big retailer's shelf, a distributor, a booking site, an app store.

Gatekeepers do bring you customers. In return, they set the terms: price, placement, fees, payment timing, rules. The more of your customers come through one gate, the more of your value they can capture.

image.label: Many small producers funneling through one gate to a crowd of customers
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 여러 작은 생산자(빵, 소스, 앱 아이콘), 가운데 좁은 문 하나와 문지기 캐릭터, 오른쪽에 많은 고객. 문지기 손에 "Terms"라고 적힌 클립보드. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Power comes from who has fewer options.
body: A gatekeeper's power is not just its size. It's the gap between your alternatives and theirs.
list: **Grocery chains:** many suppliers want limited shelf space, so some charge fees just to stock a product
**Distributors:** a region with one strong distributor sets its own margin
**App stores:** if most phones only install apps one way, the store takes a commission on many sales
cards.callout: If they can replace you easily and you can't replace them, they set the price.

cards.title: Gatekeepers aren't villains.
body: A retailer's shelf brings trust, logistics and foot traffic you could never build alone. Many brands exist only because a gatekeeper gave them a chance.
The real choice is not *gate or no gate*. It's how much of your business runs through one gate, and what you keep that's yours: customer relationships, a brand people ask for, other channels.

cards.title: Going around the gate isn't free.
body: Selling direct means you pay to find every customer yourself: ads, shipping, returns, support. That can cost more than the gatekeeper's cut.

And a second door only helps if it's real. A website that brings 2% of sales won't change a negotiation. Build alternatives early, before you need them, and judge them by how much leverage they give you, not just how they look.

cards.title: Now it's a fitness app.
body: Your workout app gets about 80% of new users through one app store's search results. The store takes a commission on subscriptions and can change its ranking rules anytime.
Profits are thin. What's your best next move?

options.text: Push users to pay elsewhere in ways that bend the store's rules
options.feedback: You might save the commission for a while, but you risk losing your main source of users overnight.

options.text: Stay in the store, but build other doors: email list, web sign-ups, gym partnerships
options.feedback: You keep the store's reach while slowly lowering how much you depend on it. It takes steady effort before it pays off.

options.text: Raise prices to cover the commission
options.feedback: It may fix margins today, but you still depend on one gate, and higher prices can slow sign-ups through it.

cards.title: Count your doors, not just the customers behind one.
body: A gatekeeper's terms get tougher as your other options shrink. Take the access, but keep something that's yours.
**Try it today:** write down what share of your sales comes through your biggest channel. If it's over half, name one step that builds a second door.
